blocks.text: **The problem.** Implement `pow(x, n)`, which calculates `x` raised to the power `n` (`xⁿ`). `n` is an integer that may be negative, as small as −2³¹.

blocks.alt: Computing 2 to the 10th by halving the exponent. pow(2, 10) needs pow(2, 5) squared; pow(2, 5) needs pow(2, 2) squared times 2, because 5 is odd; pow(2, 2) needs pow(2, 1) squared; pow(2, 1) needs pow(2, 0) squared times 2; pow(2, 0) is 1. The answers come back 1, 2, 4, 32 and 1024: five calls instead of ten multiplications.

elements.text: x^n = (x^(n/2))^2, times one more x when n is odd

elements.text: 5 calls: about log2(n), instead of n multiplications

blocks.text: The idea: divide and conquer on the exponent

Multiplying `x` by itself `n` times is O(n) — about two billion steps for the largest `n`. But `x¹⁰ = (x⁵)²`, and `x⁵ = (x²)² · x`. In general, compute `half = xⁿᐟ²` **once** and square it, multiplying by one extra `x` when `n` is odd. Each call halves the exponent, so there are only about log₂ n calls. A negative exponent means `1 / x⁻ⁿ`.
**Time O(n), space O(1).** Too slow when n is in the billions.

blocks.caption: Each call halves the exponent; the answers are squared on the way back up.

blocks.text: **Time O(log n), space O(log n)** for the call stack — 32 calls for the largest exponent. Calling `myPow(x, n / 2)` **twice** instead of storing `half` would turn the chain back into a tree with n leaves: O(n) again.
Read the exponent in binary: 10 is `1010`, so x¹⁰ = x⁸ · x². Square `x` once per bit and multiply it into the result where the bit is 1.

blocks.alt: Multiply n times: O(n) time, O(1) space. Fast power, recursive: O(log n) time, O(log n) space. Fast power, loop: O(log n) time, O(1) space.

items: **n = −2³¹** — negating it overflows a 32-bit int; use a 64-bit exponent.
**x = 1 or −1** — the answer is ±1 for any n; with n huge, only the fast versions finish.
**Super Pow** — a huge exponent given as an array of digits, everything modulo 1337.
**Modular exponentiation** — the same loop with `% m` after each multiply: the core of RSA.
**Fibonacci in O(log n)** — fast power on a 2 × 2 matrix.
